{{Short description|Definite integral of a scalar or vector field along a path}}
{{pp-pc|small=yes}}
{{More citations needed|date=June 2023}}
{{Calculus |Multivariable}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''line integral''' is an [[integral]] where the [[function (mathematics)|function]] to be integrated is evaluated along a [[curve]].<ref name="Tang2006">{{cite book|author=Kwong-Tin Tang| title=Mathematical Methods for Engineers and Scientists 2: Vector Analysis, Ordinary Differential Equations and Laplace Transforms| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kR8TqQRxbeoC&q=%22line+integral%22 | date=30 November 2006 | publisher=Springer Science & Business Media | isbn=978-3-540-30268-1}}</ref>  The terms '''''path integral''''', '''''curve integral''''', and '''''curvilinear integral''''' are also used; ''[[contour integral]]'' is used as well, although that is typically reserved for [[#Complex line integral|line integrals in the complex plane]].

The function to be integrated may be a [[scalar field]] or a [[vector field]]. The value of the line integral is the sum of values of the field at all points on the curve, weighted by some scalar function on the curve (commonly [[arc length]] or, for a vector field, the [[Dot product|scalar product]] of the vector field with a [[Differential (infinitesimal)|differential]] vector in the curve). This weighting distinguishes the line integral from simpler integrals defined on [[interval (mathematics)|intervals]]. Many simple formulae in physics, such as the definition of [[Work (physics)|work]] as {{nowrap|<math>W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{s}</math>,}} have natural continuous analogues in terms of line integrals, in this case {{nowrap|<math display="inline"> W = \int_L \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{s}) \cdot d\mathbf{s}</math>,}} which computes the [[Mechanical work|work]] done on an object moving through an electric or gravitational field {{math|'''F'''}} along a path {{nowrap|<math>L</math>.}}

== Vector calculus ==
In qualitative terms, a line integral in vector calculus can be thought of as a measure of the total effect of a given [[tensor field]] along a given curve. For example, the line integral over a scalar field (rank 0 tensor) can be interpreted as the area under the field carved out by a particular curve. This can be visualized as the surface created by {{math|1=''z'' = ''f''(''x'',''y'')}} and a curve ''C'' in the ''xy'' plane. The line integral of ''f'' would be the area of the "curtain" created—when the points of the surface that are directly over ''C'' are carved out.

=== Line integral of a scalar field ===
[[File:Line integral of scalar field.gif|frame|right|The line integral over a scalar field ''f'' can be thought of as the area under the curve ''C'' along a surface {{math|1=''z'' = ''f''(''x'',''y'')}}, described by the field. The curve end points are at <math>(x,y)=\mathbf{r}(a)</math> and <math>\mathbf{r}(b)</math>.]]
==== Definition ====
For some [[scalar field]] <math>f\colon U\to\R</math> where <math>U \subseteq \R^n</math>, the line integral along a [[piecewise smooth]] [[curve]] <math>\mathcal{C} \subset U</math> is defined as
<math display="block">\int_{\mathcal{C}} f\, ds = \int_a^b f\left(\mathbf{r}(t)\right) \left|\mathbf{r}'(t)\right| \, dt,</math>
where <math>\mathbf r\colon[a,b]\to\mathcal{C}</math> is an arbitrary [[bijective]] [[parametric equation|parametrization]] of the curve <math>\mathcal{C}</math> such that {{math|'''r'''(''a'')}} and {{math|'''r'''(''b'')}} give the endpoints of <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and {{math|''a'' < ''b''}}. Here, and in the rest of the article, the absolute value bars denote the [[Euclidean distance|standard (Euclidean) norm]] of a vector.

The function {{mvar|f}} is called the integrand, the curve <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is the domain of integration, and the symbol {{math|''ds''}} may be intuitively interpreted as an elementary [[arc length]] of the curve <math>\mathcal{C}</math> (i.e., a differential length of <math>\mathcal{C}</math>). Line integrals of scalar fields over a curve <math>\mathcal{C}</math> do not depend on the chosen parametrization {{math|'''r'''}} of <math>\mathcal{C}</math>.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web| last=Nykamp|first=Duane | title=Line integrals are independent of parametrization |url=https://mathinsight.org/line_integral_independent_parametrization | access-date=September 18, 2020|website=Math Insight}}</ref>

Geometrically, when the scalar field {{mvar|f}} is defined over a plane {{math|1=(''n'' = 2)}}, its graph is a surface {{math|1=''z'' = ''f''(''x'', ''y'')}} in space, and the line integral gives the (signed) [[Cross-section (geometry)|cross-sectional]] area bounded by the curve <math>\mathcal{C}</math> and the graph of {{mvar|f}}. See the animation to the right.

==== Derivation ====
For a line integral over a scalar field, the integral can be constructed from a [[Riemann sum]] using the above definitions of {{mvar|f}}, {{mvar|C}} and a parametrization {{math|'''r'''}} of {{mvar|C}}. This can be done by partitioning the [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] {{math|[''a'', ''b'']}} into {{mvar|n}} sub-intervals {{math|[''t''<sub>''i''−1</sub>, ''t''<sub>''i''</sub>]}} of length {{math|1=Δ''t'' = (''b'' − ''a'')/''n''}}, then {{math|'''r'''(''t''<sub>''i''</sub>)}} denotes some point, call it a sample point, on the curve {{mvar|C}}. We can use the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of sample points {{math|{'''r'''(''t''<sub>''i''</sub>): 1 ≤ ''i'' ≤ ''n''}<nowiki/>}} to approximate the curve {{mvar|C}} as a [[polygonal path]] by introducing the straight line piece between each of the sample points {{math|'''r'''(''t''<sub>''i''−1</sub>)}} and {{math|'''r'''(''t''<sub>''i''</sub>)}}. (The approximation of a curve to a polygonal path is called ''rectification of a curve,'' see [[Arc length|here]] for more details.) We then label the distance of the line segment between adjacent sample points on the curve as {{math|Δ''s''<sub>''i''</sub>}}. The product of {{math|''f''('''r'''(''t''<sub>''i''</sub>))}} and {{math|Δ''s''<sub>''i''</sub>}} can be associated with the signed area of a rectangle with a height and width of {{math|''f''('''r'''(''t''<sub>''i''</sub>))}} and {{math|Δ''s''<sub>''i''</sub>}}, respectively. Taking the [[Limit of a sequence|limit]] of the [[summation|sum]] of the terms as the length of the partitions approaches zero gives us
<math display="block">I = \lim_{\Delta s_i \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n f(\mathbf{r}(t_i)) \, \Delta s_i.</math>

By the [[mean value theorem]], the distance between subsequent points on the curve, is
<math display="block">\Delta s_i = \left|\mathbf{r}(t_i+\Delta t)-\mathbf{r}(t_i)\right| \approx \left|\mathbf{r}'(t_i) \Delta t\right| </math>

Substituting this in the above Riemann sum yields
<math display="block">I = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n f(\mathbf{r}(t_i)) \left|\mathbf{r}'(t_i)\right| \Delta t</math>
which is the Riemann sum for the integral
<math display="block">I = \int_a^b f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \left|\mathbf{r}'(t)\right| dt.</math>

=== Line integral of a vector field ===
==== Definition ====
For a [[vector field]] {{math|'''F''': ''U'' ⊆ '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> → '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>}}, the line integral along a [[piecewise smooth]] [[curve]] {{math|''C'' ⊂ ''U''}}, in the direction of '''r''', is defined as
<math display="block">\int_C \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) \,dt</math>
where {{math|·}} is the [[dot product]], and {{math|'''r''': [''a'', ''b''] → ''C''}} is a regular  [[parametric equation|parametrization]] (i.e: <math>||\mathbf{r}'(t)|| \neq0 \;\;\forall t\in[a,b]</math>) of the curve ''C'' such that {{math|'''r'''(''a'')}} and {{math|'''r'''(''b'')}} give the endpoints of ''C''.

A line integral of a scalar field is thus a line integral of a vector field, where the vectors are always [[tangential]] to the line of the integration.

Line integrals of vector fields are independent of the parametrization '''r''' in [[absolute value]], but they do depend on its [[curve orientation|orientation]]. Specifically, a reversal in the orientation of the parametrization changes the sign of the line integral.<ref name=":1" />

From the viewpoint of [[differential geometry]], the line integral of a vector field along a curve is the integral of the corresponding 1-form under the [[musical isomorphism]] (which takes the vector field to the corresponding [[covector]] field), over the curve considered as an [[Immersion (mathematics)|immersed]] 1-manifold.

==== Derivation ====
[[Image:Line integral of vector field.gif|450px|thumb|The trajectory of a particle (in red) along a curve inside a vector field. Starting from ''a'', the particle traces the path ''C'' along the vector field ''F''. The dot product (green line) of its tangent vector (red arrow) and the field vector (blue arrow) defines an area under a curve, which is equivalent to the path's line integral. (Click on image for a detailed description.)]]

The line integral of a vector field can be derived in a manner very similar to the case of a scalar field, but this time with the inclusion of a dot product. Again using the above definitions of {{math|'''F'''}}, {{mvar|C}} and its parametrization {{math|'''r'''(''t'')}}, we construct the integral from a [[Riemann sum]]. We partition the [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]] {{math|[''a'', ''b'']}} (which is the range of the values of the [[parameter]] {{mvar|t}}) into {{mvar|n}} intervals of length {{math|1=Δ''t'' = (''b'' − ''a'')/''n''}}. Letting {{math|''t<sub>i</sub>''}} be the {{mvar|i}}th  point on {{math|[''a'', ''b'']}}, then {{math|'''r'''(''t''<sub>''i''</sub>)}} gives us the position of the {{mvar|i}}th point on the curve. However, instead of calculating up the distances between subsequent points, we need to calculate their [[displacement (vector)|displacement]] vectors, {{math|Δ'''r'''<sub>''i''</sub>}}. As before, evaluating {{math|'''F'''}} at all the points on the curve and taking the dot product with each displacement vector gives us the [[infinitesimal]] contribution of each partition of {{math|'''F'''}} on {{mvar|C}}. Letting the size of the partitions go to zero gives us a sum
<math display="block">I = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t_i)) \cdot \Delta\mathbf{r}_i</math>

By the [[mean value theorem]], we see that the displacement vector between adjacent points on the curve is
<math display="block">\Delta\mathbf{r}_i = \mathbf{r}(t_i + \Delta t)-\mathbf{r}(t_i) \approx \mathbf{r}'(t_i) \,\Delta t.</math>

Substituting this in the above Riemann sum yields
<math display="block">I = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t_i)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t_i)\,\Delta t,</math>

which is the Riemann sum for the integral defined above.

=== Path independence ===
{{Main|Gradient theorem}}

If a vector field {{math|'''F'''}} is the [[gradient]] of a [[scalar field]] {{math|''G''}} (i.e. if {{math|'''F'''}} is [[Conservative vector field|conservative]]), that is,
<math display="block">\mathbf{F} = \nabla G ,</math>
then by the [[Chain rule#Multivariable case|multivariable chain rule]] the [[derivative]] of the [[function composition|composition]] of {{math|''G''}} and {{math|'''r'''(''t'')}} is
<math display="block">\frac{dG(\mathbf{r}(t))}{dt} = \nabla G(\mathbf{r} ) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)</math>
which happens to be the integrand for the line integral of {{math|'''F'''}} on {{math|'''r'''(''t'')}}. It follows, given a path ''C'', that
<math display="block">\int_C \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t)\,dt = \int_a^b \frac{dG(\mathbf{r}(t))}{dt}\,dt = G(\mathbf{r}(b)) - G(\mathbf{r}(a)).</math>

In other words, the integral of {{math|'''F'''}} over ''C'' depends solely on the values of {{math|''G''}} at the points {{math|'''r'''(''b'')}} and {{math|'''r'''(''a'')}}, and is thus independent of the path between them.  For this reason, a line integral of a conservative vector field is called ''path independent''.

=== Applications ===
The line integral has many uses in physics. For example, the [[Work (physics)|work]] done on a particle traveling on a curve ''C'' inside a force field represented as a vector field {{math|'''F'''}} is the line integral of {{math|'''F'''}} on ''C''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=16.2 Line Integrals | url=https://www.whitman.edu/mathematics/calculus_online/section16.02.html|access-date=2020-09-18|website=www.whitman.edu}}</ref>

For another example, see [[Ampère's circuital law]].

== Flow across a curve ==

For a [[vector field]] <math>\mathbf F \colon U \subseteq \R^2 \to \R^2</math>, {{math|1='''F'''(''x'', ''y'') = (''P''(''x'', ''y''), ''Q''(''x'', ''y''))}}, the '''line integral across a curve''' ''C'' ⊂ ''U'', also called the [[Flux|''flux integral'']], is defined in terms of a [[piecewise smooth]] [[parametric equation|parametrization]] {{math|'''r''': [''a'',''b''] → ''C''}}, {{math|1='''r'''(''t'') = (''x''(''t''), ''y''(''t''))}}, as:
<math display="block">\int_C \mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot d\mathbf r^\perp =
\int_a^b \begin{bmatrix} P\big(x(t),y(t)\big) \\ Q\big(x(t),y(t)\big) \end{bmatrix}
\cdot \begin{bmatrix} y'(t) \\ -x'(t) \end{bmatrix} ~dt = 
\int_a^b \left(-Q~dx + P~dy\right).</math>

Here {{math|⋅}} is the dot product, and <math>\mathbf{r}'(t)^\perp = (y'(t), -x'(t))</math> is the clockwise perpendicular of the velocity vector {{nowrap|<math> \mathbf{r}'(t) = (x'(t), y'(t))</math>.}}

The flow is computed in an oriented sense: the curve {{mvar|C}} has a specified forward direction from {{math|'''r'''(''a'')}} to {{math|'''r'''(''b'')}}, and the flow is counted as positive when {{math|'''F'''('''r'''(''t''))}} is on the clockwise side of the forward velocity vector {{math|'''r''''(''t'')}}.

== Complex line integral ==<!-- This section is linked from [[Complex plane]] -->
In [[complex analysis]], the line integral is defined in terms of [[Complex number#Multiplication|multiplication]] and [[Complex number#Addition and subtraction|addition]] of complex numbers.  Suppose ''U'' is an [[open subset]] of the [[complex plane]] '''C''', {{math|''f'' : ''U'' → '''C'''}} is a function, and <math>L \subset U</math> is a curve of finite length, parametrized by {{math|''γ'': [''a'',''b''] → ''L''}}, where {{math|1=''γ''(''t'') = ''x''(''t'') + ''iy''(''t'')}}. The line integral
<math display="block">\int_L f(z) \, dz</math>
may be defined by subdividing the [[interval (mathematics)|interval]] [''a'', ''b''] into {{nowrap|1=''a'' = ''t''<sub>0</sub> < ''t''<sub>1</sub> < ... <  ''t''<sub>''n''</sub> = ''b''}} and considering the expression
<math display="block">\sum_{k=1}^{n} f(\gamma(t_k)) \,[ \gamma(t_k) - \gamma(t_{k-1}) ] = \sum_{k=1}^n f(\gamma_k) \,\Delta\gamma_k.</math>

The integral is then the limit of this [[Riemann sum]] as the lengths of the subdivision intervals approach zero.

If the parametrization {{mvar|γ}} is [[Differentiable function#Differentiability classes|continuously differentiable]], the line integral can be evaluated as an integral of a function of a real variable:
<math display="block">\int_L f(z)\,dz = \int_a^b f(\gamma(t)) \gamma'(t)\,dt.</math>

When {{mvar|L}} is a closed curve (initial and final points coincide), the line integral is often denoted <math display="inline">\oint_L f(z)\,dz,</math> sometimes referred to in engineering as a '''cyclic integral'''.

To establish a complete analogy with the line integral of a vector field, one must go back to the definition of differentiability in multivariable calculus. The gradient is defined from [[Riesz representation theorem]], and inner products in complex analysis involve conjugacy (the gradient of a function <math>\gamma</math> at some <math>z\in\mathbb{C}</math> would be <math>\overline{\gamma'(z)}</math>, and the complex inner product would attribute twice a conjugate to <math>\gamma'</math> in the vector field definition of a line integral).

The line integral with respect to the conjugate complex differential <math>\overline{dz}</math> is defined<ref>{{cite book |first1=Lars |last1=Ahlfors |author-link=Lars Ahlfors |title=Complex Analysis |location=New York |publisher=McGraw-Hill |edition=2nd |year=1966 |page=103 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RfYK28TcZEwC&pg=PA103 }}</ref> to be
<math display="block">\int_L f(z) \overline{dz} := \overline{\int_L \overline{f(z)} \,dz} = \int_a^b f(\gamma(t)) \overline{\gamma'(t)}\,dt.</math>

The line integrals of complex functions can be evaluated using a number of techniques. The most direct is to split into real and imaginary parts, reducing the problem to evaluating two real-valued line integrals. The [[Cauchy integral theorem]] may be used to equate the line integral of an [[analytic function]] to the same integral over a more convenient curve. It also implies that over a closed curve enclosing a region where {{math|''f''(''z'')}} is analytic without [[Mathematical singularity|singularities]], the value of the integral is simply zero, or in case the region includes singularities, the [[residue theorem]] computes the integral in terms of the singularities. This also implies the path independence of complex line integral for analytic functions.

=== Example ===
Consider the function {{math|1=''f''(''z'') = 1/''z''}}, and let the contour ''L'' be the counterclockwise [[unit circle]] about 0, parametrized by {{math|1=''z''(''t'') = ''e''<sup>''it''</sup>}} with {{mvar|t}} in {{math|[0, 2''π'']}} using the [[Euler's formula|complex exponential]]. Substituting, we find:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
   \oint_L \frac {1}{z}\,dz &= \int_0^{2\pi} \frac{1}{e^{it}} ie^{it} \,dt = i\int_0^{2\pi} e^{-it}e^{it}\,dt \\
   &= i \int_0^{2\pi} dt = i(2\pi-0)= 2\pi i.
 \end{align}</math>

This is a typical result of [[Cauchy's integral formula]] and the [[residue theorem]].

=== Relation of complex line integral and line integral of vector field ===
Viewing complex numbers as 2-dimensional [[Euclidean vector|vectors]], the line integral of a complex-valued function <math>
f(z)</math> has real and complex parts equal to the line integral and the flux integral of the vector field corresponding to the [[Complex conjugate|conjugate]] function <math>\overline{f(z)}.</math> Specifically, if <math>\mathbf{r} (t) = (x(t), y(t))</math> parametrizes ''L'', and <math>f(z) = u(z) + iv(z)</math> corresponds to the vector field <math>\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \overline{f(x + iy)} = (u(x + iy), -v(x + iy)),</math> then:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
   \int_L f(z)\,dz &= \int_L (u+iv)(dx+i\,dy) \\
   &= \int_L (u,-v)\cdot (dx,dy) + i\int_L (u,-v)\cdot (dy,-dx) \\
   &= \int_L \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})\cdot d\mathbf{r} + i\int_L \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})\cdot d\mathbf{r}^\perp.
 \end{align}</math>

By [[Cauchy's integral theorem|Cauchy's theorem]], the left-hand integral is zero when <math>f(z)</math> is analytic (satisfying the [[Cauchy–Riemann equations]]) for any smooth closed curve L. Correspondingly, by [[Green's theorem]], the right-hand integrals are zero when <math>\mathbf{F} = \overline{f(z)}</math> is [[Conservative vector field|irrotational]] ([[Curl (mathematics)|curl]]-free) and [[Incompressible flow|incompressible]] ([[divergence]]-free). In fact, the Cauchy-Riemann equations for <math>f(z)</math> are identical to the vanishing of curl and divergence for {{math|'''F'''}}.

By [[Green's theorem]], the area of a region enclosed by a smooth, closed, positively oriented curve <math>L</math> is given by the integral <math display="inline"> \frac{1}{2i} \int_L \overline{z} \, dz.</math> This fact is used, for example, in the proof of the [[area theorem (conformal mapping)|area theorem]].

== Quantum mechanics ==
The [[path integral formulation]] of [[quantum mechanics]] actually refers not to path integrals in this sense but to [[functional integration|functional integrals]], that is, integrals over a space of paths, of a function ''of'' a possible path. However, path integrals in the sense of this article are important in quantum mechanics; for example, complex contour integration is often used in evaluating [[probability amplitude]]s in quantum [[scattering]] theory.
